Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I feel isolated and set apart from others

issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma in a 34-year-old Navy Officer, 'Known People: Related people' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-linked trigger without any accompanying memory or appraisal content about bereavement, loss of specific others, or interpersonal aspects of the disaster. The rest of the profile does not explain why related people would be a salient trigger.

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Evaluation' is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. It suggests social/performance shame concerns, but the negative appraisals and memory items do not involve appearance, performance failure, humiliation, or social judgment. This maladaptive strategy appears to address a symptom theme not otherwise represented.

'Avoid Friends' similarly implies socially driven withdrawal, yet the selected appraisals are global despair and alienation rather than fear of specific interpersonal consequences, and the trigger set does not include friendship or social contact themes. It is not impossible, but in combination with 'Avoid Evaluation' it pulls toward a social-evaluative formulation not supported elsewhere.

For a natural-disaster trauma in a Navy officer, 'Similar cars' is hard to connect clinically to the rest of the profile. The other triggers are generic situational reminders (crowding, locations), but this item implies a specific vehicle-related cue that is not supported by the trauma type, memory content, or appraisals.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: The negative appraisals are extremely global and severe ('life not worth living', 'belong nowhere') relative to the rest of the selected items, which focus on trauma reminders, fragmented imagery, and avoidance. This creates a coherence problem because the profile lacks corresponding threat content or broader self-concept material to support such pervasive suicidal/existential beliefs.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is especially difficult to reconcile with the demographic/contextual profile of a married Navy officer after a natural disaster unless other items indicate moral injury, social alienation, or occupational rupture; none are present in the selected components.

vignette: Three years ago, Marcus Hayes was trapped in the flooded berthing compartment of his cruiser when Category 4 winds breached the hull. Water surged past his knees, then his chest, as forty sailors pressed together in a panic. The only way out was a narrow, pitch-black corridor, and the thick stench of ruptured liquor lockers mixed with the damp air, creating a suffocating, disorienting wall. He never forgot the exact spatial layout of that crush, the way the alcohol fumes burned his throat, or the terrifying density of bodies shifting in the dark. Now, as a Lieutenant navigating the bustling corridors of the naval base, those same stimuli instantly hijack him. When he walks past a crowded mess hall or catches the faint whiff of cheap whiskey on a colleague’s breath, his mind immediately flashes to the images of the rising water and the bulkhead buckling, the sensory details sharpening into a vivid, uncontrollable replay that leaves him gasping on the spot. These sudden sensory invasions rapidly convince him that his previous joy is permanently gone, that he no longer belongs in the civilian world, and that he is fundamentally isolated from everyone around him. Because he has come to believe he is irreparably broken and set apart from normal life, his nervous system permanently maps danger to those exact doorways and scent profiles, making him fixate on spatial layouts as if they are actively hunting him. Once he accepts this devastating self-assessment, the traumatic memories stop feeling like fleeting intrusions and instead solidify into a heavy, inescapable reality he feels he must endure to make sense of his new existence. The relentless mental reliving of the drowning crowd continuously confirms his growing conviction that he is irrevocably miserable and disconnected from his past self. Because he feels his body locked in those original trapped positions every time a memory surfaces, his nervous system permanently maps danger to open spaces and alcohol scent, ensuring that any proximity to crowds or liquor instantly pulls the memory forward. When the visceral feeling of being trapped overwhelms him, he instinctively cuts off contact with his friends and retreats into the darkened storage areas of the barracks, punishing himself for surviving. His deliberate isolation and self-imposed darkness actually fuel the intensity of the reenactments, making the visual memories sharper and more inescapable, while his avoidance of light and cutting of ties creates a vacuum where any unavoidable sound of a crowded deck or faint whiskey tang becomes overwhelmingly alarming. These avoidance habits and memory reinforcements have slowly hardened into a relentless loop over the past two years, draining his marriage and costing him a promotion. He has come to believe he deserves the suffering, so he stays in the shadows, convinced that happiness is a foreign country he can never return to. The final straw came during a base-wide emergency drill; the sudden alarm and sudden crush of personnel triggered a full bodily reenactment that left him unable to move or breathe, forcing his wife to intervene. Marcus finally walked into the clinic hoping for a way to stop the suffocating cycle, though he remains terrified that stepping into the light will simply confirm he no longer belongs anywhere.
